messages.body_plain:
(a very late reply)

On 12/10/24 04:13, Jacob H wrote:
> Also, is the mapping matrix ML the correct specification for the SAM
> model with categorical items?

That is a very good question. It is certainly a convenient choice, and
perhaps closer in spirit to the IRT/ML approach, than the WLSMV approach
that we use for the CFA blocks in the first stage.

I can tell you that it seems to work very well in simulation studies, in
the sense that the resulting point estimates of the structural
parameters seem to be consistent.

The general idea is that once we have estimated the parameters in LAMBDA
and THETA (using, say, WLSMV), we don't need to worry any longer about
the categorical nature of the indicators.

But that only works if everything in the structural part can be
considered continuous. If the structural part contains some categorical
endogenous variables, then the current implementation will fail.

> Also note: I get some warnings running simulations with binary variables
> in the SAM using OLS as the structural argument struc.args =
> list(estimator = "OLS")

"OLS" is not supported (but that should trigger an error/warning). But
estimator = "ULS" does work.

> You mentioned you are in the process of writing a paper about SAM with
> categorical

I think I already have too many plans for 2025. I hope this one makes
it, but I cannot make any promises.

Yves.

On 12/12/24 11:49, 'Emma Scandolo' via lavaan wrote:
> I have a follow-up question related to the topic of this conversation. I
> am trying to figure how exactly the $res.slopes vector is estimated.

This only happens if you have exogenous covariates in your model. Vy By
default, lavaan then switches to 'conditional.x = TRUE' mode, and lavaan
will first regress out all those covariates from the endogenous
variables, before computing the thresholds and (now residual)
correlations. This is done by a series of probit regressions (one for
each dependent ordered variable), and the resulting regression
coefficients are the rows in $res.slopes.

Yves.

messages.subject_clean: Bounded Estimation in MGCFA
messages.body_plain:
Dear community,

I have a one-factor model with 3 items and I would like to conduct measurement invariance testing across 23 groups. Specifically, it will be for 23 EU countries using European Social Survey data and each country has a sample size of at least 800.

The model is as below:
CCPolSupport.Model<-'
CCPolicySupport=~support1+support2+support3
'

When I use the cfa() function to include these arguments: estimator="MLR", missing="FIML", std.lv <http://std.lv>=T, the configural invariance model could not converge.

For this reason, I try with the below code for the configural invariance model with an extra "bounds" argument (based on the code in Appendix H in this paper: De Jonckere, J., & Rosseel, Y. (2022). Using bounded estimation to avoid nonconvergence in small sample structural equation modeling. Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal, 29(3), 412-427.)

CCPolSupport.Config.Fit1.WideBound<-cfa(model =  CCPolSupport.Model  ,
                              data = ESS8,
                              group = "country",
                              estimator="MLR",
                              missing="FIML",
                              std.lv <http://std.lv>=T,
                              bounds="wide")

This works well for the configural invariance model.

However, when I tried to implement it on the full metric invariance model with an extra argument of 'group.equal="loadings"', I noticed that the bound constrains the estimate of factor variance in all groups to be 1, when in reality only the estimate of the factor variance in group 1 should be 1 and the estimate of other groups should be in reference to group 1 (e.g. 1.018 in group 2, 1.066 in group 3) .

Therefore, my questions are the below:
Is there a specific/better way to use bounded estimation correctly in the setting of MGCFA?
In terms of metric invariance model with std.lv <http://std.lv>=T, is there anyway to still use bounded estimation without constraining the estimate of factor variance in all groups to be 1?

Thank you very much in advance!

Meijun

messages.body_plain:
Hello Everyone,

I am writing to seek your expertise regarding a discrepancy I observed in the results of analyzing a confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) model. Specifically, I analyzed the model from the article Huba et al. (1981). A Comparison of Two Latent Variable Causal Models for Adolescent Drug Use using three software programs: EQS, AMOS, and Lavaan. The model involves three factors representing adolescent drug use behaviors and their associated observed variables, with some measurement errors. The complete path diagram is attached for your reference.

In EQS, the correlation matrix of parameters revealed a correlation of 3.23 between the factor loading of the "Marijuana" variable and its error term, which suggests a problematic result, possibly due to issues in data or model specification. In AMOS, this correlation was -0.97, which is also very high and indicates potential model instability or misspecification. However, in Lavaan, the correlation was reported as -0.008, which is well within the permissible range and close to zero.

I would like to understand what could explain such a significant difference in the correlation results between EQS/AMOS and Lavaan. Is it related to differences in how the three software programs handle parameter estimation, model constraints, or error correlations? Could this discrepancy be due to differences in the optimization algorithms, convergence criteria, or default settings across these software programs? Furthermore, is there a minimum cutoff value or threshold defined in the Lavaan literature to interpret correlation coefficients between parameter estimates? For instance, does Lavaan impose stricter constraints or utilize different techniques to ensure that parameter correlations do not exceed certain bounds?

Given the nature of this discrepancy and its implications for my study, I would greatly appreciate your insights and suggestions. Understanding the underlying reasons for these differences would help ensure the reliability of my analyses and allow me to interpret the results appropriately. Thank you very much for your time.

Regards,

Asghar

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

This model includes both continuous and categorical data, analyzed using multiply imputed datasets. I am first conducting a measurement invariance analysis between males and females. Once invariance is established, I will assess whether the indirect (mediational) effect significantly differs between the two groups.

measurement_model <- '
Ind1=~ x1+x2+x3+x4 #(Likert scale)
Ind2=~ z1+z2+z3+z4 #(Likert scale)
InterationInd1Ind2=~ x1z1+x2z2+x3z3+x4z4
Mediator=~ q1(continous) + q2 ( continous  ) + q3 (ordinal) + q4(ordinal)
outcome =~ y1(binary) + y2(binary)

# Modification Indices
q3~~ q4
q2~~ q3
'
fit <- cfa.mi( measurement_model   , data = imputed.data, meanstructure = TRUE, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE, estimator = "WLSMV", se = "robust", ordered = c("q3", "q4", "y1", "y2", "x1", "x2","x3","x4","z1","z2","z3","z4"))

My questions are:

Did I specify the model correctly, given that it includes an outcome with two binary variables and mixed categorical and continuous variables?
Regarding measurement invariance, there are two approaches for categorical and continuous data. What steps should I take to conduct measurement invariance for a model with mixed variables like mine?
How should I evaluate whether the indirect effect differs between groups?
When I use summary() for the model with multiply imputed data, I get average estimates only. The output is not like that of summary() with a single dataset.
I would appreciate your help in answering these questions.

Best wishes,
Ahmad

Hi, Meijun and Yago,

Lavaan (v. 0.6-19) will by default fix the first factor loadings to 1, even if they are labelled. To get around this, as Yago pointed out, you can write it as:
`CCPolicySupport  =~ L1* NA*support1 + L2*support2 + L3*support3`
If that does not work: Using "std.lv <http://std.lv>" also has the same effect, without needing to specify the NA in the first loading.

(And just in case: You can use `ParTable(CCPolSupport.Metric.Fit1.WideBound)` to make sure your parameters are all what you want them to be).

Best,
Alex

Would highly appreciate support in how this can be fixed.

Thanks a lot!

Aroob.

level: 1

diclima =~ infoclass_notlistening + infoclass_noise + infoclass_longwait

need_frustration =~ rf1 + rf2 + rf3 + rf4 + cf1 + cf2 + cf3 + cf4

external_m =~ m_7 + m_8 + m_9

intrinsic =~ m_17 + m_18 + m_19

1) modification indices should not be used without theoretical considerations, because, when you use them, you are testing a model different from your original theory.

Best,
Yago

Modification indices (and score tests more generally) are calculated as a function of first and second derivatives of the model's likelihood function, augmented with additional parameters.  Formulas are provided here, and in references contained therein:

https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/met0000243

Using (different) bounded estimation methods will change the gradient (first derivative) and Hessian (second derivative), thus changing the modification index.

> Despite the fact that X2 is different between no-bound and wide-bound estimation, epc is the same in both cases.

So it just balances out to expect the same parameter changes, despite one of your sampling methods having less uncertainty about that expected change.

messages.body_plain:
> Did I specify the model correctly, given that it includes an outcome with two binary variables and mixed categorical and continuous variables?

Looks fine, but the "outcome" factor might not be empirically identified, if its correlation with other factors is not substantial (relative to your sample size).  If you run into convergence problems or identification warnings, you can try equating its 2 indicators' loadings.

> Regarding measurement invariance, there are two approaches for categorical and continuous data.

The steps are the same, except that categorical indicators have an additional type of measurement parameter: thresholds.

> What steps should I take to conduct measurement invariance for a model with mixed variables like mine?

Start with threshold invariance, then follow the remaining steps as usual.  However, additional identification constraints complicate the process for discrete indicators.  You can use the semTools::measEq.syntax() function to help you write the appropriate syntax for each step.

> How should I evaluate whether the indirect effect differs between groups?

Establish at least partial metric invariance, so that structural parameters can be comparable across groups.  Then fit your structural model, using unique labels for the paths in each group:

https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html#constraining-a-single-parameter-to-be-equal-across-groups

Just as you define an indirect effect using the := operator:

https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/mediation.html

You can also define a new parameter that is the difference between indirect effects across groups.

> When I use summary() for the model with multiply imputed data, I get average estimates only.

That is the lavaanList-class summary method.  You can avoid this issue by using the lavaan.mi package instead (which your other post suggests you already installed--but also install the latest semTools from GitHub, so its old lavaan.mi-class does not interfere with the new one in the lavaan.mi package.

messages.subject: Re: Disagreement in bootstrapping p-value and confidence interval (SEM)
messages.subject_clean: Disagreement in bootstrapping p-value and confidence interval (SEM)
messages.body_plain:
In case others are struggling with this issue, I've written a quick and dirty script for percentile and BC intervals and p-values. The reference can be found here <https://www.statmodel.com/download/FAQ-Bootstrap%20-%20Pvalue.pdf>. Note: I have omitted any form of error handling. The functions are largely untested. At best, it's a prototype. But maybe it will be useful to someone.

Best

Christian

ci.p <- list(
  "perc" = function(t0 = NULL, t, level = 0.95) {
    M <- length(t[t < 0])
    B <- length(t)
    p <- 2 * min(M / B, 1 - M / B)
    ci <- quantile(t, c(1 - level, 1 + level) / 2, type = 6)
    return(round(c(ci, p = p), 3))
  },
  "bc" = function(t0, t, level = 0.95) {
    M <- length(t[t < 0])
    B <- length(t)
    z0 <- qnorm(length(t[t < t0]) / length(t))
    p <- 2 * if(t0 > 0) pnorm(-2 * z0 + qnorm(M / B)) else 1 - pnorm(-2 * z0 + qnorm(M / B))
    ci <- quantile(t, pnorm(2 * z0 + qnorm(c(1 - level, 1 + level) / 2)), type = 6)
    return(round(c(ci, p = p), 3))
  }
)

# Example
library(lavaan)

pop.model <- "
M ~ 0.4 * X
Y ~ 0.4 * M + 0.2 * X
"

set.seed(123)
data <- simulateData(pop.model, sample.nobs = 50)
fit <- sem(c("M~a*X", "Y~b*M+X", "ind:=a*b"), data, se = "bootstrap")

# Percentile CI. CI and p disagree
parameterEstimates(fit, boot.ci.type = "perc")

# Extract bootstraped coefs (quick and dirty - using bootstrapLavaan would be better)
boot <- data.frame(fit@boot$coef)
colnames(boot) <- names(coef(fit))

# CI and p do not disagree
ci.p[["perc"]](t = boot$a * boot$b)

# BC-CI. CI and p disagree
parameterEstimates(fit, boot.ci.type = "bca.simple")

# CI and p do not disagree
ci.p[["bc"]](t0 = coef(fit, type = "user")["ind"], t = boot$a * boot$b)

I am trying to replicate the method described in this paper, but in R (Propensity Score Analysis With Latent Covariates: Measurement Error Bias Correction Using the Covariate’s Posterior Mean, aka the Inclusive Factor Score. DOI: 10.3102/1076998620911920) . The paper uses MPlus to fit the structural equation model.

Example:
I want to obtain an estimate of E[U|W,X,A] where latent factor (U) with indicators (let's just say there are 3) W=(W1, W2, W3). I want the estimate to be conditional on A and X, where X which is a cause of U and A, and U is a cause of A . For simplicity, assume the indicators W are independent of each other, A, and X (conditional on U). A is a binary variable but all others are continuous.

I believe I could specify this model as:
U =~ W1 + W2 + W3
A ~ U + X
U ~ X
U ~~ 1*U
(but please let me know if this does not match up with the scenario I described, as I am still new to this).

Then, I want to fit the model using maximum likelihood and obtain estimates of the posterior mean E[U|W,A,X] conditional on A and X as well as W.

What I've found in the documentation:
In the lavaan documentation for lavPredict, I see that the possible methods are "In the linear case (when the indicators are continuous), the possible options are "regression" or "Bartlett". In the categorical case, the two options are "EBM" for the Empirical Bayes Modal approach, and "ML" for the maximum likelihood approach." (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lavaan/lavaan.pdf page 60).  I don't see anything about obtaining estimates of the posterior mean.

I suppose an alternative to lavaan is blavaan, but the method I want to replicate is not inherently bayesian so it might require more work for me to understand if this is a big deviation from what I intended to do. But I see in the blavaan documentation (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/blavaan/blavaan.pdf) that the blavInspect method has an option to return the estimated posterior mean. An additional question is how the predictions in the blavPredict (with type = "lv") function are computed -- would this also give me the posterior mean. Maybe I should use blavaan with non-informative priors? But again, I don't think this is ideal, and I'm also worried about computation time, as I'm also planning on doing some simulations, and  my very general understanding is that bayesian methods can sometimes take a while.

Any help would be much appreciated! For reference, I am a graduate student working with latent variables and structural equation models for the first time. So I apologize if my question is ill-posed or if the answer to this question is available somewhere already.

Thank you,
Grace
